procedural_history.impugned_order: The High Court accepted the contention and held that the respondent was guilty of contempt of court and directed him to pay a fine of Rs. 500 and costs.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Allahabad praying for appropriate writs quashing the order of suspension. He alleged that the appellant had no authority to pass the order and that the order was made in bad faith. On the same date the respondent obtained an ex parte order from the High Court staying the operation of the suspension order. After hearing both the parties the High Court vacated the stay order. The respondent filed a petition in the High Court asking for committal of the appellant for contempt of court. His contention was that the appellant had launched a parallel inquiry in the matter he had committed contempt of court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The respondent filed an appeal after obtaining special leave from the Supreme Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether an authority holding a disciplinary inquiry in good faith is guilty of contempt of court merely because a parallel inquiry on the same issue is pending before a court.

facts: A college principal was suspended, and he filed a writ petition in the High Court to challenge the suspension.
He initially obtained an ex-parte stay against the continuation of the disciplinary inquiry, but the High Court later vacated this stay order.
After the stay was vacated, the college manager served a charge-sheet on the principal to proceed with the inquiry.
The principal then filed a petition arguing that the manager was in contempt of court for starting a parallel inquiry while the writ petition was still pending.
The High Court agreed and held the manager guilty of contempt.
law: To constitute contempt of court, an act must be calculated to obstruct or interfere with the due course of justice or lower the court's authority.
Disciplinary proceedings and court proceedings are distinct. The disciplinary authority has the power to inquire into an employee's conduct, a power which civil or criminal courts do not possess.
The mere pendency of a court proceeding does not automatically bar a disciplinary authority from taking action.
An authority holding an inquiry in good faith, using powers given by statutory regulations, is not guilty of contempt simply because a parallel inquiry is pending in a court.
The disciplinary authority is free to exercise its lawful powers unless there is a specific stay order from a court preventing it from doing so.
application: The Supreme Court found that the disciplinary inquiry into the employee's guilt and the court proceeding were separate matters handled by different authorities with different powers.
It cited several precedents establishing that a bona fide domestic or departmental inquiry is not contempt of court, even if it runs parallel to a criminal trial on the same charges.

The Court determined that the manager acted in good faith. A crucial factor was that the High Court had explicitly vacated the stay order, giving the manager a reasonable belief that the disciplinary proceedings could continue.

The Court found no evidence that serving the charge-sheet was intended to interfere with the court proceedings. On the contrary, it suggested the principal instituted the contempt proceeding with the ulterior motive of delaying the inquiry after failing to secure a stay.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the idea that a parallel inquiry automatically constitutes contempt. It concluded that an authority holding a disciplinary inquiry in good faith is not guilty of contempt of court merely because a related matter is pending in court. Since the manager acted in good faith after the court's stay was lifted and was not obstructing justice, he was not in contempt. The Court therefore allowed the appeal and overturned the High Court's decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether a disciplinary authority is free to proceed with its inquiry in the absence of a stay order from a court, even when the subject matter is pending before that court.

facts: An employee (respondent) was suspended pending a disciplinary inquiry.
The employee filed a petition in the High Court to challenge the suspension and obtained an initial ex-parte stay order against the inquiry.
After hearing both parties, the High Court vacated the stay order.
Following the vacation of the stay, the disciplinary authority (appellant) served a charge-sheet on the employee to continue the inquiry.
The employee then initiated contempt of court proceedings, arguing that the authority could not proceed with the inquiry while the main petition was still pending in court.
law: The power to take disciplinary action is vested in the disciplinary authority, not in a civil or criminal court.
The initiation and continuation of disciplinary proceedings in good faith is not considered an obstruction or interference with the course of justice in a pending court case.
A parallel inquiry by a domestic tribunal into charges against an employee does not, by itself, amount to contempt of court, even if the same charges are pending before a civil or criminal court.
It is the employee's responsibility to move the court and obtain a specific order restraining (a stay order) the disciplinary proceedings.
application: The Court reasoned that the disciplinary authority and the court have separate and distinct powers. The pendency of a court case does not automatically bar the disciplinary authority from exercising its lawful power to conduct an inquiry.
The Court rejected the broad idea that any parallel inquiry automatically amounts to contempt. It emphasized that for an action to be contempt, it must be a willful violation of a court order.
In this case, the High Court had explicitly vacated the stay order. This meant there was no active order preventing the disciplinary authority from proceeding.

Therefore, by serving the charge-sheet after the stay was lifted, the authority was acting within its rights and in the bona fide belief that it could continue the proceedings. It was not willfully violating any court order.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that in the absence of a specific stay order from a court, a disciplinary authority is free to exercise its lawful powers and proceed with its inquiry, even if the subject matter is pending before that court. The mere pendency of the court proceeding does not act as an automatic bar, and proceeding with the inquiry without a stay does not constitute contempt of court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an authority holding a disciplinary inquiry in good faith is guilty of contempt of court merely because a parallel inquiry on the same issue is pending before a court.
appellant_arguments: An inquiry by a domestic tribunal conducted in good faith into charges against an employee does not amount to contempt of court, even if an inquiry into the same charges is pending before a court.
The service of the charge-sheet was made in good faith and was not intended or calculated to interfere with the court proceedings.
respondent_arguments: Launching a parallel inquiry into a matter that is the subject of a pending writ petition constitutes contempt of court.
A parallel inquiry on a matter that is sub judice is bound to interfere with the even and ordinary course of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a disciplinary authority is free to proceed with its inquiry in the absence of a stay order from a court, even when the subject matter is pending before that court.
appellant_arguments: The disciplinary authority had a bona fide belief that the proceedings could be continued after the High Court vacated the stay order.
respondent_arguments: The disciplinary inquiry should not proceed as the subject matter is pending before the court, regardless of whether a specific stay order is in effect.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An inquiry by a domestic tribunal in good faith into the charges against an employee does not amount to contempt of court merely because an inquiry into the same charges is pending before a civil or criminal court. In the absence of a stay order, the disciplinary authority is free to exercise its lawful power.
obiter: The initiation and continuation of disciplinary proceedings in good faith is not calculated to obstruct or interfere with the course of justice in the pending court proceedings.
The civil or criminal court has no power to take disciplinary action, as such power is vested in the disciplinary authority.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An authority holding an inquiry in good faith in exercise of the powers vested in it by statutory regulations is not guilty of contempt of Court merely because a parallel inquiry is pending before a Court. The initiation and continuation of disciplinary proceedings in good faith is not calculated to obstruct or interfere with the course of justice in the pending court proceeding, as the issue in a disciplinary proceeding (an employee's guilt on a charge) is distinct from the matters decided by a civil or criminal court. In this specific case, the appellant acted in good faith, with the bona fide belief that proceedings could continue after the High Court vacated the stay order, and the respondent instituted the contempt proceeding with ulterior motives to delay the inquiry.
legal_tests_applied: To constitute contempt of court, there must be involved some 'act done or writing published calculated to bring a court or a judge of the court into contempt or to lower his authority' or 'something calculated to obstruct or interfere with the due course of justice or the lawful process of the court.'
policy_considerations: The power of taking disciplinary action is vested in the disciplinary authority, and a civil or criminal court has no such power. An employee seeking to halt such proceedings must move the court for a stay order. In the absence of a stay order, the disciplinary authority is free to exercise its lawful powers. A parallel inquiry by a domestic tribunal does not necessarily amount to contempt of court.
